title: Four Indian Space Startups Ride SpaceX's Transporter-18 to Orbit
excerpt: TakeMe2Space's MOI-1A, Dhruva Space's LEAP-2, SatLeo's TAPAS-1 and EON's MIRA imaging system all reached orbit aboard the October 1 rideshare from Vandenberg.
body:
• SpaceX's Transporter-18 dedicated rideshare lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, on October 1, delivering 130 payloads to low-Earth orbit.
  • Four Indian ventures rode the same flight: TakeMe2Space's MOI-1A orbital-computing satellite, Dhruva Space's LEAP-2 hosted platform, SatLeo Labs' TAPAS-1 thermal imager, and EON Space Labs' MIRA multispectral system.
  • All payloads were authorized by IN-SPACe; chairperson Pawan Goenka called it a "genuinely big day for India's private space sector," noting India now has around 450 space startups.
  • Notable co-passenger: Google's "Project Suncatcher," a TPU test prototype built with Planet that was announced by Sundar Pichai in late September.

Vandenberg, California: A SpaceX Falcon 9 lifted off from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base at 18:32 UTC on October 1, carrying 130 payloads to low-Earth orbit — among them four Indian ventures, in what regulators are calling a landmark day for the country's private space sector.

The mission, Transporter-18, was a dedicated smallsat rideshare flight. The first-stage booster landed back at Landing Zone 4 on its 25th flight — SpaceX says its rideshare program has now deployed more than 1,800 payloads. But for India, the headline was the density of its own private-sector presence on a single international flight.

The four Indian payloads

TakeMe2Space's MOI-1A (Hyderabad) is a 14-kg satellite carrying Nvidia Orin NX edge processors with 117 TOPS of onboard computing, 2 TB of storage and a nine-band multispectral imager. It runs customer AI models in orbit — the company claims this cuts the volume of data that must be downloaded by a factor of 1,000. With 23 customers signed, 80 percent of them outside India, MOI-1A replaces MOI-1, which was lost in the failed PSLV-C62 launch in January 2026. The company plans MOI-1B on ISRO's SSLV in November, two more satellites in 2027, and a six-satellite constellation completed on SpaceX flights in late 2028, targeting roughly $6 million in annual recurring revenue by 2028.

Dhruva Space's LEAP-2 (Hyderabad) is a "Launching Expeditions for Aspiring Payloads" hosted platform built on the company's P-30 bus, carrying four hosted payloads — including France's Sodern HORUS star tracker from ArianeGroup and SatLeo's TAPAS-1. The P-30 bus was space-qualified on PSLV-C58 in January 2024, and LEAP-1 flew on a Falcon 9 in August 2025. Dhruva has raised about $24 million in equity, venture debt and grants, including a Rs 105-crore RDI grant for its 500-kg-class Project Garud.

SatLeo Labs' TAPAS-1 (Ahmedabad), a CubeSat-class payload flown as a hosted payload on LEAP-2, is described as India's first commercial thermal imaging payload from a private company. It uses long-wave infrared sensing to measure land-surface temperature, a stepping stone toward a proposed PYRO constellation of 10 to 15 satellites by 2029. The eight-to-thirty-person company raised a $2.2 million seed round from Unicorn India Ventures in April 2026 and is running pilot programs in Ahmedabad and Tumakuru.

EON Space Labs' MIRA (Hyderabad) is a compact 502-gram multispectral imaging system integrated aboard MOI-1A itself, capturing multi-band imagery for agriculture, mining, marine, supply-chain and insurance applications.

The regulatory milestone

All four payloads were authorized by IN-SPACe, India's space-sector regulator. Chairperson Pawan Goenka called it a "genuinely big day for India's private space sector" and noted that India now has roughly 450 space startups, about 20 of them ready to scale.

"Genuinely big day for India's private space sector."

— Pawan Goenka, chairperson, IN-SPACe

His post on X also noted the mission carried "two Indian satellites and an Indian hosted payload" — an understated tally of a flight on which Indian hardware flew both independently and nested inside other Indian satellites.

What next

The commercial logic is tightening fast. Transporter-18's Indian payloads represent three different business models — orbital computing (TakeMe2Space), hosted platforms (Dhruva), thermal sensing (SatLeo), and piggyback imaging (EON) — all reaching orbit on the same rideshare ticket. With MOI-1B targeting an ISRO SSLV launch next month and SatLeo's TAPAS-2 planned for 2027, the question for India's private space sector is no longer whether it can reach orbit, but whether it can convert rideshare access into recurring revenue before the global smallsat market consolidates.
